reason: The sources contain rich, cross-verified details about M30's discovery, core collapse, extreme stellar density, and vampire blue straggler stars.
story: In 1764, comet hunter Charles Messier spotted a faint smudge in the constellation Capricornus and logged it as a starless nebula. He was looking at Messier 30, a massive, 13-billion-year-old globular cluster containing hundreds of thousands of stars. But deep inside, Messier 30 holds a chaotic secret. Its inner core underwent a gravitational meltdown known as core collapse. Densely packing half its mass into a sphere just 17 light-years across, stars began crowding together at extreme densities. In this stellar traffic jam, old stars collided or entered tight binary loops. Some acted like cosmic vampires, leeching mass and hydrogen fuel from their neighbors. This sudden influx of fresh hydrogen rejuvenated the aging suns, creating blue stragglers—vampire stars that defy cosmic aging by burning bright, hot, and blue long after they should have died. Hubble images now reveal this stellar fountain of youth hidden in deep space.
angle: In the collapsed core of Messier 30, aging stars act like cosmic vampires by siphoning mass from neighboring stars to cheat death and reverse their aging process.

claims.claim: Messier 30 (also known as NGC 7099) is a globular cluster located in the constellation Capricornus.
Charles Messier discovered M30 in 1764 and cataloged it as a round nebula containing no stars.
William Herschel was the first astronomer to resolve Messier 30 into individual stars in the 1780s.
Messier 30 spans approximately 90 to 93 light-years in diameter.
Messier 30 is an ancient star cluster estimated to be roughly 12 to 13 billion years old.
Messier 30 has undergone a gravitational process called core collapse, creating an extraordinarily dense central region.
The collapsed core of Messier 30 has a physical diameter of only about 0.9 light-years.
Half of Messier 30's total mass is concentrated within a central sphere roughly 17.4 light-years in diameter.
Messier 30 is one of about 21 globular clusters in the Milky Way known to have experienced core collapse.
The dense conditions in Messier 30's core cause high rates of stellar interactions, collisions, and binary star formation.
Messier 30 contains blue straggler stars that appear hotter, bluer, and younger than the surrounding old star population.
Blue stragglers in Messier 30 can form when a star acts like a vampire, siphoning hydrogen mass from its companion in a binary system.
Observations from the Hubble Space Telescope helped astronomers identify two distinct types of blue stragglers in Messier 30.
Messier 30 is approaching our region of space at a velocity of roughly 181 to 185 kilometers per second.

disputed: Distance to Messier 30: S3 cites 22,800 light-years (7,000 parsecs), whereas S1, S2, S4, and S5 cite distances between 27,100 and 28,000 light-years. Script should use the widely agreed range of 27,000 to 28,000 light-years.
Best viewing window: S1 specifies August, S2 lists October, and S3 states April through January. Script should avoid naming a single best month unless properly attributed.
